opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of my favorite examples, because it captures something we've been chasing for a long time: consistency over time, or a kind of world memory.

The setup is simple. You're in a generated environment, you paint some strokes on a wall, then you turn away so the wall is completely out of view. You look around, maybe for a minute, and then you turn back. The paint is still there, in the same place and in the same shape. That sounds trivial, because in a game engine it would be. But Genie 3 has no explicit 3D representation underneath. There's no mesh, no NeRF, no Gaussian splat, no stored scene graph. It generates the world frame by frame, autoregressively, conditioned on what came before and on the user's actions.

So when the model renders that wall again, it isn't fetching an object from memory. It has to have learned, purely from training, that the world should persist and that what you did earlier should still be reflected. Earlier world models, including our own previous versions, would often forget things like that, or the scene would drift once something left the frame. You'd turn around and the room would be subtly different. Getting consistency to hold for around a minute was a real step change, and we didn't hand-engineer it. It emerged with scale and with the right training setup.

It matters beyond looking cool, too. If you want to use these models to train embodied agents, the world has to be consistent. An agent can't learn cause and effect if its actions don't have lasting consequences. If it paints a wall, moves an object, or opens a door, that change has to persist, or the agent can't learn anything meaningful. So that demo is a small window into what makes world models viable as training environments for more general agents.

There's plenty left to do. The consistency horizon is still limited, and we'd love to extend it from minutes to much longer. But that paint example was one of the moments where the team thought, okay, something qualitatively different is happening here.

r001.rationale: It says the paint remains after the view turns away and explains that earlier actions should still be reflected in the generated world.

r002.rationale: It discusses training embodied and general agents, but does not suggest vocational uses.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that one's actually one of my favorite examples, and it's a nice illustration of what we mean when we talk about consistency or memory in a world model. So the setup is you're in a generated world, you walk up to a wall, you paint something on it, you turn around, you walk away, you come back, and the strokes are still there, exactly as you left them.

Why that matters is that nothing in the architecture was explicitly designed to do that. There's no scene graph, there's no explicit 3D representation of the wall being stored somewhere. It's an autoregressive model generating frames one at a time, and the only way it can get that right is by effectively remembering what happened earlier in the context and reproducing it when it's relevant again. So that's an emergent capability, and it's one of the things that really changed between Genie 2 and Genie 3. With Genie 2 you could look away and things would drift or morph, and that's fine for a short clip, but it's not fine if you want an environment an agent can actually interact with over minutes.

And the painting case is kind of a stress test for that, because it's an arbitrary, user-generated change to the world. It's not something the model could have memorised from training data, like "doors stay where doors are." The user made a mark that's never existed anywhere before, and the model has to treat it as part of the state of the world now. That's really the crux of it. If you want to use these things for training agents, the agent needs to be able to take an action, have it change the world, and then have that change persist so it can reason about the consequences. Otherwise you're just generating pretty video, you're not simulating.

So for me it was significant partly because it's a visible, intuitive demonstration that a general audience gets immediately, and partly because it tells us something about where the scaling is taking us. We didn't hand-engineer memory. It came out of training a bigger model on more data with a real-time constraint, and it suggests that a lot of the properties we'd want from a world simulator can come from the same recipe.

r001.rationale: It says the user-created painted strokes remain after walking away and returning, showing that the world preserves the consequences of an action.

r002.rationale: It discusses training interactive agents, but does not suggest vocational uses.

astra-6.text:
What’s striking is that the model seems to maintain a persistent world, rather than just generate a plausible next frame. You paint something, look away, and when you come back, those strokes are still there. So your action has changed the environment in a way that survives being out of view.

That’s a really important property for an interactive world model. If things reset or change every time you turn around, it’s hard to do anything meaningful over time. This demonstration gives us a concrete example of that consistency. It doesn’t establish that the model has perfect memory or tell us exactly how it represents the world, but it’s a compelling step toward environments where actions have lasting consequences.

r001.rationale: It says the painted strokes remain after looking away and returning, showing that an action changes the environment in a way that persists.

r002.rationale: It discusses interactive world models and lasting consequences, but does not suggest any vocational uses.
